opus-5.5.text:
I think it built up gradually, almost without me noticing. Each time I stepped into something where I really didn't know if it would work out, whether that was moving to a new country for school, switching research directions, or starting on a problem nobody around me had solved yet, there was this period of real discomfort. You feel lost, you question whether you belong there. But then you get through it, not always successfully, but you get through it, and you realize the world didn't end.

After going through that cycle a few times, what changes isn't so much that you become sure you'll succeed. It's more that you become comfortable with not knowing. You develop a kind of trust in your own process: okay, I've been confused before, I've been the person in the room who understood the least, and I figured out how to learn my way out of it. That's a very different kind of confidence than believing you're talented. It's confidence that you can adapt.

And I think that matters a lot in research especially, because by definition you're working on things where the answer isn't known. If you need certainty before you commit, you'll never start anything interesting. So for me, repeatedly taking on those uncertain challenges taught me that the uncertainty itself is not a signal to stop. It's usually a signal that you're in the right place to learn something.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradually gaining confidence in her ability to adapt through uncertainty, but it does not clearly say she recognized in retrospect that she could accomplish many things independently.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it didn't happen the way people usually imagine, where you take on something hard, you succeed, and then you feel confident. It was messier than that.

When I started doing robot learning research, almost nothing worked the first time. You'd spend months building a system, and the robot would just fail in some way you hadn't even anticipated. So early on, I don't think I gained confidence from succeeding. What I gained was a kind of tolerance for not knowing whether something would work, and still being willing to commit to it anyway.

The thing that shifted over time wasn't really "I know I can do this." It was more like "I know what it feels like to be lost, and I know I can usually find my way out." That's a different kind of confidence. It's not about the outcome, it's about trusting your own process. Every uncertain project I took on gave me another data point that confusion is a normal phase and not a signal to stop.

And I'd say the "on my own" part is interesting, because I actually learned that being independent doesn't mean doing everything alone. Taking on hard problems repeatedly taught me when to push through myself and when to go ask someone who's seen it before. Knowing the difference is probably the real skill. The confidence isn't that I can solve anything single-handedly, it's that I can figure out what the next step should be, even when I have no idea what the final answer looks like.

r001.rationale: The response describes confidence developing over time and explains that independence can include asking others for help. It does not say the speaker recognized only in retrospect that they could accomplish many things independently.

astra-6.text:
I think it helped me build confidence gradually. When you take on something uncertain, you don’t know at the beginning whether you can do it. But you try, you get stuck, and you figure out a next step. After doing that repeatedly, you have some evidence that being unsure doesn’t mean you’re incapable.

So the confidence becomes less about, “I can do everything on my own,” and more about, “I can find a way forward.” That includes recognizing when I need help and asking for it. I can still take responsibility for the challenge without having all the answers myself.

r001.rationale: It describes confidence building through repeated attempts and finding a way forward, including asking for help, but does not say she recognized in retrospect that she could accomplish many things independently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think confidence comes from going through that uncertainty and realizing you can still take the next step. You might not know how to solve the whole problem, but you can learn something, try something, and adjust when it doesn’t work. After doing that repeatedly, the unfamiliar feels less intimidating.

It’s not that I became certain I could do everything on my own. I became more comfortable trusting my judgment—and recognizing when I needed to ask for help. For me, those two things go together.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated uncertainty made unfamiliar challenges less intimidating and that she learned to trust her judgment while asking for help. It does not say she recognized only in retrospect that she could accomplish many things independently.
